stem: A 34-year-old weightlifter felt a pop in his lower back during a heavy deadlift and had immediate pain that now runs down the back of his left thigh and calf to the foot. It worsens with coughing and sitting. A straight left leg raise at 40 degrees reproduces the pain. He has no saddle numbness or bladder trouble, and x-rays show normal vertebrae and alignment.
oneliner: 34M + weightlifter + pop during deadlift + immediate back pain radiating down posterior left leg to foot + worse cough, sitting + positive left straight-leg raise + no saddle numbness, bladder trouble + normal x-ray → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains his leg pain?

options.A: Nucleus pulposus pushed through a torn annulus fibrosus onto a nerve root
options.B: A compression fracture of a vertebral body pressing on the cord
options.C: Strain of the paraspinal muscles
options.E: Forward slippage of one vertebra over another

whyNot.B: **X-rays show normal vertebrae**; no saddle or bladder signs of cord/cauda compression
whyNot.C: Gives **local pain and spasm**, not pain down the leg with a positive straight-leg raise
whyNot.D: Would give **weakness and sensory loss** in the whole sciatic distribution, no cough effect
whyNot.E: **Spondylolisthesis**: visible slip on x-ray; alignment is normal

answer: Posterolateral disc herniation compressing a nerve root (sciatica)
why: **Heavy axial load tears the annulus**, and the **nucleus pulposus bulges out posterolaterally** onto a **nerve root**. **Radicular pain below the knee, a positive straight-leg raise, and worse pain on coughing** are typical.

idea.rule: Sudden back pain with leg pain below the knee after lifting is a disc herniation compressing a nerve root.
also: L4-L5 and L5-S1 are most common
Midline herniation with saddle anesthesia and bladder trouble is cauda equina: emergency
Posterior longitudinal ligament makes the herniation posterolateral

stem: A 71-year-old man has back pain and notes that his hat size has increased. Serum alkaline phosphatase is 1,145 U/L, with normal calcium and phosphorus. A radiograph of the lumbar spine is shown.
oneliner: 71M + back pain + larger hat size + ALP 1,145 + normal Ca and P + spine radiograph → what starts the process?
ask: Which of the following is the initiating abnormality?

options.C: Excess PTH driven bone resorption
options.E: Failure of osteoclast acid secretion

whyNot.A: That is **osteoporosis** (normal ALP, no bone enlargement)
whyNot.C: PTH excess causes **hypercalcemia** and subperiosteal resorption; his calcium is normal
whyNot.D: **Osteomalacia**: low calcium or phosphorus and Looser zones
whyNot.E: That is **osteopetrosis**: dense but brittle bone, in young patients with marrow failure

answer: Excessive osteoclast activity starts the disorganized bone remodeling
why: Paget disease begins with **excess osteoclast activity** (**RANKL-driven**, often **SQSTM1** mutation). Osteoblasts compensate with disorganized **woven bone**, giving **thick, weak bone** and a very high **alkaline phosphatase**.

idea.rule: Paget disease: osteoclast overactivity comes first, then chaotic osteoblast repair lays down weak woven bone.
also: Lytic phase: osteoporosis circumscripta of the skull
Mixed phase: mosaic pattern of cement lines
Sclerotic phase: picture-frame or ivory vertebra
Bisphosphonates help by blocking osteoclasts

image.prompt: Lateral radiograph of the lumbar spine showing vertebral bodies with thickened, sclerotic cortical margins giving a picture-frame appearance, with coarsened trabeculae. No text or labels.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has had 5 months of morning stiffness lasting over an hour, with symmetric swelling of her wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints and ankles. ESR is elevated and rheumatoid factor is positive. She has no history of atopy.
oneliner: 29F + 5 mo morning stiffness >1 h + symmetric swelling of wrists, MCPs, ankles + high ESR + RF positive → key mediators?
ask: Which of the following mediators most directly drives her synovial inflammation and joint destruction?

options.C: IL-4 and IL-5
options.E: IL-10

whyNot.B: Mediates **allergy**; she has no atopy
whyNot.D: Signature cytokine of **SLE**; she has symmetric small-joint synovitis with RF
whyNot.E: Is **anti-inflammatory**

answer: TNF and IL-1 from synovial macrophages drive inflammation and joint destruction
why: In rheumatoid arthritis, **macrophages and Th1/Th17 cells** in the synovium release **TNF-alpha and IL-1**, which drive **synovitis, pannus formation** and **bone and cartilage destruction**. This is why **TNF inhibitors** work.

idea.rule: RA synovitis and erosions are driven by TNF and IL-1 (with IL-6) from the synovium.
also: TNF blockers: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab
Anakinra blocks IL-1
Tocilizumab blocks the IL-6 receptor
RANKL from synovial cells drives osteoclast erosions

stem: A 52-year-old man has had recurrent episodes of severe pain and swelling at the base of the great toe, and now has firm nodules on both elbows. Serum uric acid is 7.9 mg/dL and creatinine is normal. He takes no diuretics or aspirin. He drinks 5 to 6 beers every day.
oneliner: 52M + recurrent great-toe attacks + elbow nodules + uric acid 7.9 + normal creatinine + no diuretics or aspirin + 5-6 beers daily → how does drinking raise urate?
ask: Which of the following best explains how his drinking raises serum urate?

options.C: Lactate competing with urate for secretion in the proximal tubule
options.E: Increased tubular urate reabsorption from volume contraction by diuretics

whyNot.A: Blocking xanthine oxidase **lowers** urate; that is how allopurinol works
whyNot.B: An **inherited childhood** defect (Lesch-Nyhan) with self-injury, not caused by drinking
whyNot.D: His **creatinine is normal**, so filtration is intact
whyNot.E: He **takes no diuretics**

answer: Alcohol-derived lactate competes with urate for proximal tubular secretion (plus faster purine turnover)
why: Ethanol metabolism raises **NADH**, so pyruvate becomes **lactate**. Lactate and other organic acids **compete with urate for the proximal tubule anion transporters**, so less urate is excreted. Alcohol also **speeds ATP breakdown to purines**, and beer adds purines, so **tophaceous gout** follows.
chain: Lactate competes with urate at proximal tubule transporters
Less urate excreted, serum urate rises
Urate crystals: gout attacks and tophi

idea.rule: Anything that adds organic acid anions to the blood reduces renal urate excretion.
also: Lactic acidosis
Ketoacidosis (diabetic, starvation)
Low-dose aspirin
Thiazide and loop diuretics (via volume contraction and transporter competition)

stem: A chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan extract from cartilage is dried and weighed. When placed in saline, the extract swells to many times its dry volume and then springs back after being compressed.
oneliner: Dried chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan + placed in saline → swells many times and rebounds after compression → which property?
ask: Which property best explains this behavior?

options.C: A high density of negative charges attracting counter-ions and water
options.E: A high content of positively charged lysine residues

whyNot.A: Anchors the matrix but **does not draw in water**
whyNot.B: Hydrophobic residues would **repel water**
whyNot.D: Gives **rigidity**, not swelling
whyNot.E: GAGs are **negatively** charged; positive charge would not attract cations and water

answer: Sulfate and carboxylate groups give a dense negative charge, binding cations and water
why: Chondroitin sulfate has **many sulfate and carboxylate groups**, so the proteoglycan carries **dense negative charge**. These attract **cations and water (osmotic pull)** and repel one another, so it **swells and resists compression**, cushioning joints.

idea.rule: Negatively charged GAGs bind water, giving cartilage its cushion.
also: Aggrecan: core protein with chondroitin and keratan sulfate
Hyaluronic acid forms the backbone of aggregates
Osteoarthritis loses proteoglycan and water

stem: A 14-year-old girl has a long leg cast for 6 months after a tibial fracture. When it is removed, her calf is 2 cm smaller than the other side and the muscle feels weak. CK is normal, nerve conduction studies are normal, and she has no pain or rash.
oneliner: 14F + long leg cast 6 months + calf 2 cm smaller + weak + normal CK + normal nerve conduction → process in the muscle cells?
ask: Which process best explains the loss of muscle mass?

options.A: Increased ubiquitin tagging and proteasomal degradation of myofibrillar proteins
options.C: Loss of dystrophin from the sarcolemma
options.D: Death of the lower motor neuron
options.E: Lysosomal glycogen accumulation

whyNot.B: **Myositis**: pain, raised CK, and inflammatory infiltrate
whyNot.C: **Duchenne**: boys, raised CK, and **both legs**, from early childhood
whyNot.D: **Denervation**: fasciculations, and abnormal nerve studies
whyNot.E: **Pompe**: infant onset and cardiomegaly

answer: Disuse atrophy: unloading activates the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway
why: Without load, muscle activates **atrogin-1 and MuRF1** (E3 ligases), so proteins are **tagged with ubiquitin** and broken down by the **proteasome**. Fibers shrink without damage, so **CK stays normal**.

idea.rule: Disuse atrophy = proteasomal protein breakdown, not fiber death.
also: Same pathway in sepsis, cancer cachexia, steroids
Regain mass with resistance training
Denervation atrophy: group atrophy and fasciculations

stem: A 2-year-old boy has short arms and legs but a normal trunk length, a large head with a prominent forehead, a flattened midface and a low nasal bridge. His hands are short with a trident appearance and his intelligence is normal. Both parents are of average height, and his father is 46 years old. X-rays show short, thick long bones.
oneliner: 2M + short limbs, normal trunk + large head, frontal bossing + flat midface + trident hands + normal intelligence + parents average height, father 46 → defect?
ask: Which mechanism best explains his short limbs?

options.C: Activating FGFR3 mutation inhibiting growth plate chondrocyte proliferation
options.E: Defective mineralization from low vitamin D

whyNot.A: **Osteogenesis imperfecta**: fractures, blue sclerae, hearing loss; limbs not rhizomelic
whyNot.B: **GH deficiency**: proportionate short stature, no skull changes
whyNot.D: **Osteopetrosis**: dense, brittle bones and anemia
whyNot.E: **Rickets**: bowing, widened growth plates, low calcium or phosphate

answer: Gain-of-function FGFR3 mutation impairs endochondral ossification
why: A **gain-of-function FGFR3 mutation** (often de novo, with **older fathers**) **inhibits chondrocyte proliferation** in the growth plate. **Endochondral bone growth fails** so limbs are short, but **membranous bone** (skull, face) grows normally.

idea.rule: Achondroplasia impairs endochondral, not membranous, bone formation.
also: Autosomal dominant with high de novo rate
Normal intelligence and lifespan, risk of spinal stenosis
Membranous bone formation: skull and clavicle

stem: An isolated frog skeletal muscle is placed in a glucose-rich bath with oxygen limited and is stimulated to contract repeatedly until force falls. Lactate and inorganic phosphate in the fibres have risen.
oneliner: Experiment: isolated muscle + glucose bath + repeated stimulation until force falls, lactate and Pi up → which variable fell?
ask: Which intracellular variable has decreased at the onset of this fatigue?

options.C: ADP
options.E: Ammonia

whyNot.B: Rises, as stated, as creatine phosphate and ATP are broken down
whyNot.C: Rises as ATP is used faster than it is made
whyNot.E: Rises as AMP is deaminated in working muscle

answer: Intracellular pH falls (lactic acid and H+ accumulate)
why: Repeated contraction outpaces oxidative supply, so **anaerobic glycolysis** makes lactate and **H+**. The **falling pH** (with raised Pi) impairs cross-bridge cycling and calcium handling.
chain: Acidosis and Pi impair cross-bridges and Ca2+ handling

idea.rule: Muscle fatigue comes from metabolic change inside the fibre (H+, Pi, ADP, substrate loss), not from ATP running out.
also: Raised inorganic phosphate
Raised ADP
Reduced sarcoplasmic Ca2+ release
Glycogen depletion in prolonged exercise

stem: A 66-year-old man has a titanium prosthesis placed in the hip for osteoarthritis. Six weeks later, imaging shows new bone growing into the prosthesis surface.
oneliner: 66M + hip arthroplasty + new bone growing into prosthesis at 6 wk → which cell secretes the collagen matrix?
ask: Which cell secretes the type I collagen matrix at this interface?

options.C: Chondroblast
options.E: Mast cell

whyNot.A: A **resting** cell trapped in matrix; maintains bone, does not lay it down
whyNot.D: **Resorbs** bone; it is multinucleated and macrophage-derived
whyNot.E: A **connective tissue** immune cell; no matrix production

answer: Osteoblasts secreting type I collagen osteoid
why: **Osteoblasts** lay down **type I collagen (osteoid)**, which then mineralises with hydroxyapatite. Some become **osteocytes** trapped in the matrix.
chain: Osteoblasts secrete type I collagen osteoid

idea.rule: Osteoblasts build bone (osteoid, ALP, osteocalcin); osteoclasts remove it.
also: Fracture callus formation
Bone growth at epiphyseal plates
Osteoid in osteomalacia is unmineralised
Osteoblasts release RANKL to drive osteoclasts

stem: In a physiology laboratory, strips of skeletal muscle are fixed at rest and at maximal contraction and examined by electron microscopy. Sarcomere length falls from 2.4 to 1.6 micrometres, and filament lengths are unchanged.
oneliner: Experiment: skeletal muscle fixed at rest and at maximal contraction, sarcomere 2.4 to 1.6 um, filament lengths unchanged -> which region nearly vanishes?
ask: Compared with the resting fibres, which region has almost disappeared?

options.C: H zone
options.E: Thick filament length

whyNot.A: Its length is the **thick filament length**, unchanged in contraction
whyNot.B: Persists as the **sarcomere boundary**; the lines move closer together
whyNot.D: Persists at the **centre of thick filaments**
whyNot.E: Filaments **do not shorten**; they slide

answer: H zone
why: Cross-bridges pull **thin filaments toward the M line**, so the thin filaments overlap the centre. The **H zone (thick filaments only)** and I band shorten, while the **A band stays constant**.
chain: Thin and thick filaments overlap more
H zone and I band shorten
H zone nearly vanishes; A band unchanged

idea.rule: In contraction filaments slide; filament lengths do not change.
also: I band also shortens
A band is constant
Sarcomere shortens as Z lines approach
In stretch the H zone and I band widen

stem: In an experiment on a large skeletal muscle fibre, the action potential travelling along the surface membrane is followed by near-simultaneous contraction of myofibrils deep in the fibre, far too fast for diffusion.
oneliner: Experiment: surface action potential then synchronous contraction of deep myofibrils, too fast for diffusion → how is excitation conducted inward?
ask: Which mechanism carries excitation inward?

options.B: Na+/K+ pumping by the sarcoplasmic reticulum
options.C: Diffusion of calcium from the sarcolemma
options.E: Action potential spread along T tubules

whyNot.A: Myofibrils are **not electrically coupled**; they sit inside one cell
whyNot.B: The SR pumps **Ca2+ (SERCA)**, not Na+/K+, and cannot conduct excitation
whyNot.C: Far **too slow**, and Ca2+ is released from the SR
whyNot.D: Skeletal muscle fibres are **not coupled** by gap junctions

answer: Transmission along T tubules
why: **T tubules** are invaginations of the sarcolemma that carry the **action potential** deep into the fibre. **DHP receptors** sense the voltage and **ryanodine receptors** release Ca2+ from the SR.
chain: Ryanodine receptors release Ca2+ from the SR

idea.rule: T tubules bring the surface action potential to the SR so the whole fibre contracts in unison.
also: Cardiac T tubules also trigger calcium-induced calcium release
Mutated DHP receptor causes hypokalemic periodic paralysis
Malignant hyperthermia: ryanodine receptor defect
Triads (T tubule with two SR cisternae) in skeletal muscle, dyads in cardiac

stem: A newborn girl is born without limbs. Genetic testing finds a loss-of-function mutation in an FGF receptor expressed in limb bud mesenchyme.
oneliner: Newborn + absent limbs + FGF receptor mutation in limb mesenchyme → which process failed?
ask: Which process was most directly impaired?

options.C: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal conversion
options.E: Neural crest migration

whyNot.A: Occurs **later** to separate digits; its failure gives syndactyly
whyNot.B: Cannot explain **absent limb outgrowth**
whyNot.C: Not the FGF step in limb **outgrowth**
whyNot.E: A **craniofacial and PNS** process, not limb outgrowth

answer: Proliferation of the underlying limb mesenchyme
why: The **apical ectodermal ridge** secretes **FGF**, which drives **mesenchyme proliferation** and proximodistal outgrowth. Without FGF signalling the limb does not grow.

idea.rule: Limb development is directed by signalling centres: AER-FGF for outgrowth, ZPA-Shh and dorsal Wnt-7 for patterning.
also: Shh from ZPA: anteroposterior axis
Wnt-7 from dorsal ectoderm: dorsoventral axis
Holt-Oram syndrome (TBX5): limb and heart defects
Thalidomide: limb bud damage (phocomelia)

stem: A 24-year-old woman had a closed humeral shaft fracture treated in a brace 3 weeks ago. She feels well, and the fracture is united by a callus on x-ray. Serum calcium and phosphate are normal.
oneliner: 24F + closed humeral fracture 3 wk ago + callus on x-ray + normal Ca and phosphate → which lab is raised?
ask: Which serum value is most likely raised?

options.C: Creatine kinase
options.E: Parathyroid hormone

whyNot.B: Stated normal; healing does not **raise** serum calcium
whyNot.C: Rises with **muscle injury**, mostly in the first days
whyNot.D: A **liver and biliary** marker, not bone
whyNot.E: No reason to rise when **calcium is normal**

answer: Alkaline phosphatase from osteoblast activity
why: Fracture healing builds a **callus** by **osteoblasts**, which release **alkaline phosphatase** into the blood, so serum ALP rises while calcium stays normal.

idea.rule: Raised ALP with normal Ca and GGT points to bone formation.
also: Paget disease of bone
Osteomalacia and rickets
Osteoblastic metastases
Normal growth in adolescents

stem: Cultured fibroblasts are given radiolabeled proline and lysine. Newly made pro-alpha chains are collected and found to contain hydroxyproline and glycosylated hydroxylysine. This has already happened before the chains assemble into a triple helix and before procollagen is packaged into secretory vesicles.
oneliner: Experiment: fibroblasts + labeled proline and lysine → chains hydroxylated and glycosylated before triple helix and before vesicle packaging → which compartment?
ask: In which compartment do these modifications occur?

options.C: Extracellular space
options.E: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum

whyNot.A: Procollagen reaches it only for **packaging into vesicles**, after these modifications
whyNot.C: **Procollagen peptidases and lysyl oxidase** act outside the cell, later than these steps
whyNot.D: Degrades material; the chains here are **newly made** and headed for secretion
whyNot.E: Makes **lipids and detoxifies**; it has no ribosomes to make pro-alpha chains

answer: Rough endoplasmic reticulum
why: Pro-alpha chains are made on **ribosomes of the rough ER**. There **proline and lysine are hydroxylated** (needs **vitamin C**), **hydroxylysine is glycosylated**, and the **triple helix** forms before procollagen goes to the Golgi and out of the cell.
chain: Pre-pro-alpha chains synthesized on rough ER

idea.rule: Collagen is modified inside the cell first, then cross-linked outside.
also: Scurvy: low vitamin C impairs hydroxylation
Ehlers-Danlos syndromes: defects in collagen processing or structure
Osteogenesis imperfecta: defective type I collagen
Lysyl oxidase cross-links outside the cell and needs copper

stem: Researchers incubate tropoelastin made by cultured aortic smooth muscle cells with a copper-dependent enzyme that oxidizes side-chain amino groups to aldehydes. After acid hydrolysis they isolate desmosine, a four-armed ring that holds neighboring chains together and gives the fiber its recoil.
oneliner: Tropoelastin + copper-dependent enzyme oxidizing side-chain amino groups to aldehydes + four-armed desmosine ring after hydrolysis → which residue supplies the arms?
ask: Side chains of which amino acid condense to form this cross-link?

options.C: Glycine
options.E: Cysteine

whyNot.B: Proline's side chain is a closed ring with **no free amino group** for the enzyme to oxidize
whyNot.C: Glycine has **no side chain** at all, so it cannot become an arm of the ring
whyNot.D: Hydroxyproline carries a **hydroxyl, not an amino group**, on its side chain; it stabilizes the collagen triple helix
whyNot.E: Cysteine's side chain is a **thiol**, which forms disulfide bonds; it is not an **amino group oxidized to an aldehyde**

answer: Lysine
why: **Lysyl oxidase** (copper-dependent) turns the side-chain amino group of **lysine** into an aldehyde. **Four lysine residues** from neighboring chains then condense into **desmosine**, the cross-link that gives lung and aorta their **elastic recoil**.
chain: Lysyl oxidase oxidizes lysine side chains to aldehydes
Four lysines from neighboring chains condense

idea.rule: Lysyl oxidase makes cross-links from lysine in both collagen and elastin.
also: Collagen cross-links: lysine and hydroxylysine, also via lysyl oxidase
Menkes disease: low copper leaves lysyl oxidase inactive, so vessels and hair are fragile
Lathyrism (beta-aminopropionitrile) inhibits lysyl oxidase and weakens the aorta
Desmosine and isodesmosine each join four lysine side chains

stem: A 24-year-old man wakes unable to lift his legs after a long run and a large pasta dinner the evening before. His arms are weak too, reflexes are reduced, and sensation is normal. He is alert and has no muscle pain or dark urine. Similar episodes have occurred three times this year, and his strength is normal between them.
oneliner: 24M + flaccid weakness after hard exercise and a carbohydrate meal + reduced reflexes, normal sensation, no myalgia + normal between episodes → serum change in an attack?
ask: Which serum change is most likely during an attack?

options.A: Raised potassium released from injured muscle cells
options.B: Low calcium causing tetany and muscle spasm
options.C: Low potassium, shifted into muscle cells
options.E: Raised creatine kinase from muscle breakdown

whyNot.A: Hyperkalemic attacks follow **potassium-rich food or fasting**; a **large carbohydrate meal** raises insulin and drives potassium into cells
whyNot.B: Hypocalcemia gives **spasm and brisk reflexes**, not flaccid weakness with **reduced reflexes**
whyNot.D: Needs excess intake or renal failure; it does not recur as **episodes after a carbohydrate meal**
whyNot.E: Rhabdomyolysis brings **pain and dark urine**; he has neither and is **strong between attacks**

answer: Hypokalemia from potassium moving into muscle cells
why: A channel mutation (**CACNA1S**, less often SCN4A) lets **potassium shift into muscle** after insulin surges such as a carbohydrate meal or exercise recovery. The **low serum potassium** leaves the membrane inexcitable, so weakness is **flaccid with reduced reflexes** and clears between attacks.
chain: Trigger: carbohydrate meal or exercise raises insulin and adrenaline
Potassium shifts from plasma into muscle cells
Flaccid weakness, reduced reflexes, then recovery

idea.rule: In hypokalemic periodic paralysis the potassium is moved, not lost, so total body stores stay normal.
also: Insulin and beta-agonists also push potassium into cells
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis is the same picture with hyperthyroidism
Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis is set off by potassium intake or fasting
Acetazolamide helps prevent attacks

stem: A 63-year-old woman, ten years past menopause and never on hormone therapy, has sudden mid-back pain after lifting a laundry basket. Imaging shows a compressed vertebral body. Serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase are all normal, and her DEXA T-score is -3.1.
oneliner: 63F + 10 years postmenopausal, no hormones + vertebral compression fracture after light lifting + normal Ca, phosphate, ALP + T-score -3.1 → what drives the bone loss?
ask: Which change in bone signalling best explains her bone loss?

options.A: More osteoblast RANKL with less osteoprotegerin decoy
options.B: Raised osteoprotegerin secreted by osteoblasts, blocking RANKL
options.C: Lower RANKL expression on osteoblasts, slowing osteoclasts
options.D: Raised PTH driven by a low serum calcium level
options.E: Defective osteoid mineralization from lack of vitamin D

whyNot.B: Excess osteoprotegerin would **block osteoclasts** and raise bone mass; estrogen loss **lowers** it
whyNot.C: Estrogen loss **raises RANKL**; a fall in RANKL would reduce resorption
whyNot.D: Her **calcium is normal**, so there is no stimulus for secondary PTH
whyNot.E: That is **osteomalacia** with low calcium or phosphate and **high alkaline phosphatase**; hers are normal

answer: Increased RANKL with decreased osteoprotegerin
why: Estrogen normally restrains osteoblast RANKL and supports osteoprotegerin (the decoy receptor). After menopause **RANKL rises and osteoprotegerin falls**, so **RANK on osteoclast precursors** is overstimulated and resorption outpaces formation. Mineral and alkaline phosphatase values stay normal.
chain: RANK signalling on osteoclast precursors increases
Trabecular bone is lost; vertebral fracture

idea.rule: Bone mass depends on the RANKL to osteoprotegerin ratio; osteoporosis tips it toward resorption.
also: Denosumab is an antibody against RANKL
Bisphosphonates induce osteoclast apoptosis
Osteoporosis labs are normal, unlike osteomalacia or Paget
Glucocorticoids also raise RANKL and lower osteoprotegerin

stem: A 29-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis has taken oral prednisone almost continuously for three years. She now has sudden low back pain after bending to lift a bag. Imaging shows a compressed vertebra, and serum calcium is normal. A bone biopsy shows thinned but normally mineralized trabeculae with few active osteoblasts.
oneliner: 29F + ulcerative colitis + 3 years of prednisone + vertebral compression fracture on minor load + normal calcium + thin, mineralized trabeculae, few osteoblasts → main mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism chiefly explains her bone loss?

options.A: Increased osteoblast activity producing disorganized woven bone
options.C: Excess parathyroid hormone from the parathyroid glands
options.D: Failed osteoclast resorption leaving dense, brittle bone
options.E: Suppressed osteoblast differentiation and bone formation

whyNot.A: Woven bone from overactive osteoblasts fits **Paget disease**; here osteoblasts are **few**
whyNot.B: That gives **osteomalacia** with soft, unmineralized osteoid; her trabeculae are **normally mineralized**
whyNot.C: Primary hyperparathyroidism brings **high calcium**; hers is **normal**
whyNot.D: Osteoclast failure is **osteopetrosis**, with **dense** bone; hers is thin

answer: Reduced osteoblast bone formation
why: Glucocorticoids **suppress osteoblast differentiation and survival**, so new bone formation falls. They also **reduce gut calcium absorption**, raise urinary calcium loss and increase resorption, leaving **thin trabeculae** that fracture under light load.
chain: Gut calcium absorption falls, urinary calcium rises

idea.rule: Steroid bone loss is mainly a formation problem, hitting trabecular bone first.
also: Vertebrae and ribs fracture earliest
Fracture risk rises within 3 to 6 months of starting prednisone
Bisphosphonates with calcium and vitamin D protect during long courses
Cushing syndrome produces the same bone loss

stem: A 45-year-old woman asks about her osteoporosis risk because her mother broke a hip at 70. Her menstrual periods are still regular. She is 168 cm tall and weighs 48 kg. She plays tennis twice a week and gardens most days, eats a diet rich in dairy, and drinks two cups of coffee daily.
oneliner: 45F + mother with hip fracture + regular periods + BMI about 17 + tennis and gardening + dairy-rich diet + 2 coffees daily → which feature most increases her risk?
ask: Which of the following most increases her risk of osteoporosis?

options.B: Low body weight for her height
options.C: High dietary calcium intake from dairy products
options.D: Moderate daily caffeine intake of two cups of coffee
options.E: Regular weight-bearing exercise such as tennis and gardening

whyNot.A: Regular cycles mean **normal estrogen**, which restrains resorption and **protects** bone
whyNot.C: Adequate calcium supports mineralization and is **protective**, not harmful
whyNot.D: Only **heavy** caffeine intake has a weak link; two cups has **no meaningful effect**
whyNot.E: Mechanical loading **stimulates bone formation**, so her exercise is **protective**

answer: Low body weight
why: Bone responds to **mechanical load**: body weight and weight-bearing activity stimulate osteoblast formation. A **low body weight** means less load and less estrogen from fat, so peak and maintained bone mass are lower. Her **exercise and calcium intake protect** her.
chain: Less mechanical load on the skeleton
Less stimulus for osteoblast bone formation
Lower peak and maintained bone mass

idea.rule: Load builds bone; anything that reduces skeletal loading or estrogen lowers bone mass.
also: Low BMI, anorexia nervosa and the female athlete triad
Prolonged bed rest and spaceflight cause rapid loss
Weight-bearing exercise (not swimming) protects
Obesity lowers risk of osteoporosis though not of other fractures

stem: A 68-year-old woman has knee pain on stairs, and an x-ray shows narrowed joint space. A sample of her articular cartilage tested under compression is softer than normal. Her collagen fibrils are intact, but the matrix has lost much of its water-binding capacity.
oneliner: 68F + knee pain on stairs + joint space narrowing + cartilage softer under compression + collagen fibrils intact, matrix holds less water → which component failed?
ask: Loss of which matrix component best explains the reduced compressive stiffness?

options.A: Type II collagen fibrils forming the tensile network
options.B: Type I collagen fibers as found in tendon and bone
options.C: Elastin fibers that allow recoil of stretched tissue
options.E: Fibronectin linking cells to extracellular matrix

whyNot.A: Collagen supplies **tensile strength**, and her fibrils are **intact**
whyNot.B: Hyaline cartilage is built on **type II**, not type I; and her **collagen fibrils are intact**
whyNot.C: Elastin gives **recoil**, is scant in hyaline cartilage, and does not **bind water**
whyNot.E: Fibronectin mediates **cell adhesion**; it does not **bind water** or resist compression

answer: Negatively charged proteoglycans (aggrecan) that hold water
why: **Aggrecan** carries many negatively charged glycosaminoglycans that **attract and hold water**, so cartilage resists compression. **Type II collagen** supplies tensile strength. In osteoarthritis proteoglycan loss softens the matrix.
chain: Fewer fixed negative charges in the matrix
Matrix holds less water under load

idea.rule: In cartilage, collagen resists stretch and proteoglycans resist squeeze.
also: Hyaline cartilage matrix is type II collagen
Aggrecan binds hyaluronate and link protein
Cartilage is avascular and heals poorly
Chondroitin and keratan sulfate are the main glycosaminoglycans

stem: A 12-year-old boy with a BMI above the 97th percentile has three months of vague left knee pain and a limp. The left hip has limited internal rotation, and the thigh rotates outward as the hip is flexed. An x-ray shows the femoral head sitting posteriorly and inferiorly on the neck, with no fracture line through the metaphysis. He has no fever and is otherwise well.
oneliner: 12M + obese + 3 months of knee pain and limp + hip internal rotation limited, thigh rotates outward on flexion + head sits posterior-inferior on x-ray → which injury?
ask: Which type of injury best describes this lesion?

options.A: Salter-Harris type II, through the physis and part of the metaphysis
options.B: Avascular necrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis
options.C: Salter-Harris type I, through the physis
options.D: Traction apophysitis at the tibial tubercle
options.E: Transient synovitis of the hip after a viral illness

whyNot.A: Type II leaves a **metaphyseal fragment**; his x-ray shows **no metaphyseal fracture line**
whyNot.B: Legg-Calve-Perthes affects **younger, small** boys with a dense, flattened head, not a slipped one
whyNot.D: That causes pain at the **front of the knee** in athletes, with a normal hip
whyNot.E: Gives a **brief** painful hip in a younger child with a **normal x-ray**; his head has **slipped** and pain has lasted **3 months**

answer: Salter-Harris type I fracture through the proximal femoral growth plate
why: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is a **Salter-Harris type I** fracture through the **hypertrophic zone of the proximal femoral physis**. The epiphysis stays in the acetabulum while the neck moves **anterior and superior**, so the head appears **posterior and inferior**. Obesity and early adolescence load the physis.
chain: Obesity and growth spurt load the physis
Shear across the hypertrophic zone of the growth plate
Epiphysis slips posteriorly and inferiorly on the neck
Internal rotation lost; thigh rotates outward on flexion
Knee or thigh pain from obturator nerve referral

idea.rule: SCFE is a physeal slip: the neck moves out and up while the head stays put.
also: Referred knee pain from the hip is the classic trap
Obesity and endocrine disease (hypothyroidism) are risks
Salter-Harris I is through the physis only (SALTR: Slipped)
Treat with in-situ pinning and non-weight-bearing

stem: A 52-year-old man develops a hot, swollen right knee overnight. Aspirated fluid shows needle-shaped crystals. His left hand has two firm white nodules over the finger joints. Serum urate is 9.8 mg/dL, and his 24-hour urinary uric acid excretion is low-normal. He is not on any medication.
oneliner: 52M + abrupt hot swollen knee + needle crystals + tophi on the hand + urate 9.8 + low-normal 24-h urinary urate → main cause of the high urate?
ask: Which mechanism most often causes hyperuricemia in a patient like this?

options.A: Reduced renal tubular excretion of urate
options.C: Increased PRPP synthetase activity increasing purine synthesis
options.D: Increased cell turnover from a hematologic malignancy
options.E: Excess intestinal absorption of dietary purines

whyNot.B: Lesch-Nyhan is a **childhood** disease with self-mutilation, and gives **high urinary urate**
whyNot.C: A rare **overproducer** state; his **low-normal urinary urate** points away from overproduction
whyNot.D: Causes **high urinary urate**, and he has no cytopenias or other features
whyNot.E: Diet adds only a **small share**; it does not explain tophi with low-normal urinary urate

answer: Underexcretion of uric acid by the kidney
why: About **90% of primary gout is renal underexcretion**, with only a minority from overproduction. A **low-normal 24-hour urinary urate** with a high serum level fits underexcretion; overproducers excrete **more than 800 mg/day**.
chain: Monosodium urate crystals deposit in joints and soft tissue

idea.rule: Most gout is a kidney problem: too little urate leaves, not too much made.
also: Thiazides, loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin and niacin lower excretion
Overproduction: HGPRT deficiency, PRPP synthetase excess, tumor lysis
Alcohol and lactic acid also compete for excretion
24-hour urine over 800 mg suggests overproduction

stem: A 2-year-old girl starts crying and will not use her right arm after her father yanks her up by the hand as she stumbles on a curb. The arm hangs slightly bent and turned palm down. There is no swelling, bruising or deformity, and she lets him touch the shoulder and wrist freely.
oneliner: 2F + yanked up by the hand + holds arm slightly flexed and pronated + no swelling or deformity + will not use arm → which injury?
ask: Which injury is most likely?

options.A: Supracondylar fracture of the distal humerus
options.B: Olecranon fracture of the proximal ulna
options.C: Avulsion of the medial epicondyle apophysis
options.D: Posterior dislocation of the elbow joint
options.E: Radial head subluxation

whyNot.A: Follows a **fall on the outstretched hand** with swelling and pain; here the cause is **traction**
whyNot.B: Needs a **direct blow or fall** onto the elbow with swelling and bruising
whyNot.C: Arises from **valgus stress or throwing** with focal medial swelling and tenderness
whyNot.D: Follows **major trauma** with marked **deformity**, which is absent

answer: Radial head subluxation (nursemaid elbow)
why: A sudden **longitudinal pull on the extended, pronated arm** pulls the **radial head partly out from under the annular ligament** in a child under about 5, whose ligament is lax. The child holds the arm **flexed and pronated** with **no swelling or deformity**.
chain: Sudden traction on extended pronated arm
Annular ligament slips over the head and traps
Arm held slightly flexed and pronated

idea.rule: Nursemaid elbow is a ligament slipping over the radial head, not a broken bone.
also: Peak age is 1 to 4 years
Annular ligament encircles the radial head
Reduction is by supination with flexion or by hyperpronation
Fractures show swelling, bruising and bone tenderness

stem: A 20-year-old man playing football grabbed an opponent's shirt as the opponent ran past, and his finger was pulled straight. Now he cannot bend the tip of his right ring finger. When the other fingers are held straight he can still flex the middle joint of that finger, but the tip stays straight. The fingertip is tender and swollen at the base.
oneliner: 20M + football, finger pulled straight while gripping + cannot flex ring-finger tip + middle joint flexion intact + tender at base → which tendon injury?
ask: Which injury is most likely?

options.C: Extensor tendon avulsion at the distal phalanx
options.D: Central slip rupture of the extensor tendon
options.E: Rupture of the A2 pulley of the flexor sheath

whyNot.A: This would stop **middle-joint** flexion; his is **intact**
whyNot.C: Mallet finger leaves the tip **drooped and unable to extend**, not unable to flex
whyNot.D: Boutonniere deformity: **middle joint flexed**, tip hyperextended, and he can bend it
whyNot.E: Pulley rupture causes **bowstringing** with flexion still possible; he **cannot flex the tip** at all

answer: Avulsion of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon
why: Forced extension of an **actively flexing fingertip** tears the **flexor digitorum profundus** off the distal phalanx, most often in the **ring finger**. Profundus alone flexes the **DIP**, so with the PIP held straight the tip cannot flex while **PIP flexion by the superficialis stays intact**.
chain: Sudden forced extension at the fingertip
Profundus tendon torn from distal phalanx

idea.rule: Profundus flexes the fingertip; superficialis flexes the middle joint.
also: Test profundus by flexing the DIP with the PIP held straight
Test superficialis by holding the other fingers straight
The ring finger is involved in about three quarters of cases
Mallet finger is the opposite lesion, an extensor injury

stem: A 55-year-old woman has had right shoulder pain for six weeks since starting overhead weight training. Pain is worst on lifting the arm to the side, with tenderness just below the lateral edge of the acromion. Passive motion is full. Resisted abduction at 90 degrees with the thumbs pointing down is painful and weak.
oneliner: 55F + new overhead weight training + lateral shoulder pain on abduction + tender below acromion + full passive motion + empty-can test positive → which tendon?
ask: Which tendon is most likely impinged?

options.C: Teres minor
options.E: Long head of biceps

whyNot.A: Causes weak **external rotation** with the elbow at the side
whyNot.B: Weakens **internal rotation** and gives a positive lift-off test
whyNot.C: An **external rotator**; it does not abduct, so it would not weaken **resisted abduction**
whyNot.E: Causes **anterior** pain over the bicipital groove; her tenderness is **lateral, below the acromion**

answer: Supraspinatus tendon
why: The **supraspinatus** starts abduction and runs **under the acromion** to the greater tuberosity, so repeated overhead abduction pinches it. The **empty-can test** isolates it, and **passive motion stays full**.
chain: Pain and weakness at 60 to 120 degrees abduction

idea.rule: The tendon that starts abduction is the one that gets pinched under the acromion.
also: Rotator cuff: SITS (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis)
Supraspinatus: abduction 0 to 15 degrees; empty-can test
Infraspinatus and teres minor: external rotation
Subscapularis: internal rotation; lift-off test

stem: A 79-year-old woman slips on a rug and cannot get up. Her left leg is shorter than the right and the foot points outward. An x-ray shows a fracture between the greater and lesser trochanters of the left femur.
oneliner: 79F + fall at home + left leg shortened, foot turned outward + fracture between the trochanters → which muscle turns the foot out?
ask: Which muscle most directly accounts for the outward turning of the foot?

options.C: Piriformis
options.E: Rectus femoris

whyNot.A: It is a **medial rotator**, so it would turn the foot **inward**
whyNot.B: An **adductor**; it does not **laterally rotate** the hip
whyNot.D: A **medial rotator** and abductor of the thigh, so it would turn the foot **inward**
whyNot.E: A **hip flexor and knee extensor**, not a rotator

answer: Piriformis
why: After the fracture the **lateral rotators** (**piriformis**, obturators, gemelli, quadratus femoris) act **unopposed** and turn the leg outward, while the thigh muscles pull the limb proximally. The result is a **shortened, externally rotated leg**.
chain: Fracture disrupts the femoral neck and trochanteric region
Thigh muscles pull the limb upward

idea.rule: Hip fracture: the leg is short and turned out because the lateral rotators win.
also: Lateral rotators: piriformis, obturators, gemelli, quadratus femoris
Femoral neck fractures also give a short, externally rotated leg
Posterior hip dislocation gives a short, internally rotated leg
Gluteus medius and minimus abduct and medially rotate
